item.content:encoded:
ロサンゼルス・ドジャースの大谷翔平が、2026年のMLBポストシーズンに臨む。
本記事では、大谷翔平の2026年MLBポストシーズン出場見通しをはじめ、二刀流の可能性、ドジャースの試合日程を紹介する。
大谷翔平は2026年MLBポストシーズンに出場する？
ロサンゼルス・ドジャースの大谷翔平は、2026年のMLBポストシーズンに出場する見通しとなっている。
大谷は右上腕の炎症により9月8日付で15日間の負傷者リスト(IL)に入っていたが、9月23日(現地時間)に戦列へ復帰。復帰後も指名打者(DH)として出場を続けている。
デーブ・ロバーツ監督も「一番大事なのは健康な状態でプレーできたこと。いい状態で迎えられる」と語っており、ポストシーズンでも打者として主力出場する見通しだ。
大谷翔平はポストシーズンで二刀流出場する？
大谷の2026年シーズンにおける投手登板はすでに終了しているため、ポストシーズンでは指名打者(DH)に専念する予定となっている。
そのため、10月のポストシーズンで投手として登板する予定はなく、打者としてドジャース打線を牽引することになる。
ドジャースに所属する日本人選手
2026年のドジャースには、大谷翔平、山本由伸、佐々木朗希の日本人選手3名が所属している。
| 選手 | ポジション |
|---|---|
| 大谷翔平 | 指名打者(DH) |
| 山本由伸 | 投手 |
| 佐々木朗希 | 投手 |
ドジャースのMLBポストシーズン試合日程
ドジャースはナショナル・リーグ西地区で優勝し、第2シードを獲得したため、ワイルドカードシリーズが免除される。
ポストシーズンはナ・リーグ地区シリーズ(NLDS)から登場し、ブレーブスvsフィリーズのワイルドカードシリーズ勝者と対戦する。
ナ・リーグ地区シリーズ(NLDS)
| 試合 | 日程(日本時間) | 開催 |
|---|---|---|
| 第1戦 | 2026年10月4日(日) | ホーム |
| 第2戦 | 2026年10月5日(月) | ホーム |
| 第3戦 | 2026年10月7日(水) | アウェー |
| 第4戦 ※必要な場合 | 2026年10月8日(木) | アウェー |
| 第5戦 ※必要な場合 | 2026年10月10日(土) | ホーム |
ドジャースが地区シリーズを突破した場合の日程
ドジャースが地区シリーズを勝ち抜いた場合は、ナ・リーグ優勝決定シリーズ(NLCS)へ進出する。
NLCSは7戦4勝制で、日本時間10月12日(月)から10月20日(火)まで開催予定となっている。
さらにNLCSを突破した場合はワールドシリーズへ進出。ワールドシリーズは日本時間10月24日(土)に開幕し、最長で11月1日(日)まで行われる予定だ。
| ラウンド | 日程(日本時間) | 方式 |
|---|---|---|
| ナ・リーグ優勝決定シリーズ(NLCS) | 2026年10月12日(月)～10月20日(火) | 7戦4勝制 |
| ワールドシリーズ(WS) | 2026年10月24日(土)～11月1日(日) | 7戦4勝制 |
MLBポストシーズン2026のテレビ放送・ネット配信予定
MLBポストシーズン2026は、Amazonプライムビデオ『SPOTVチャンネル』、『SPOTV NOW』『MLB.tv(Amazonあり)』『Lemino(SPOTVパック)』でネット配信されるほか、衛星放送『J SPORTS』でも中継が予定されている。
『NHK』でもポストシーズンの注目試合が放送される予定だ。
| チャンネル | 形態 | ポストシーズン中継 |
|---|---|---|
| SPOTVチャンネル(Amazon) [30日間無料体験あり] | ネット | ポストシーズン厳選試合、ワールドシリーズ全試合をライブ配信 【ワイルドカードシリーズ】 9/30(水)6:00 ホワイトソックスvsアストロズ 10/1(木)6:00 ホワイトソックスvsアストロズ 10/2(金)6:00 ホワイトソックスvsアストロズ 【ディビジョンシリーズ】 未発表 【リーグチャンピオンシップシリーズ】 未発表 【ワールドシリーズ】 全試合 |
| J SPORTS | 衛星放送 | 注目試合を生中継 【アストロズ vs ホワイトソックス】 9/30(水)5:50 第1戦 10/1(木)5:50 第2戦 10/2(金)5:50 第3戦 【パドレス vs カブス】 9/30(水)10:50 第1戦 10/1(木)10:50 第2戦 10/2(金)10:50 第3戦 |
| MLB.tv(Amazon) [7日間無料トライアルあり] | ネット | 全試合をライブ配信 |
| SPOTV NOW | ネット | 全試合をライブ配信 |
| Lemino(SPOTVパック) | ネット | 全試合をライブ配信 |
| NHK 総合・総合サブ | 地上波 | 注目試合を生中継 9/30(水)10:50 カブスvsパドレス |
| NHK BS | 衛星放送 | 注目試合を生中継 10/1(木)10:59 カブスvsパドレス |
| NHK BSプレミアム4K | 衛星放送 | 注目試合を生中継 9/30(水)10:50 カブスvsパドレス |
※各チャンネルの中継対象試合は各ラウンド対戦カード決定後に発表。
MLBポストシーズン2026のおすすめ視聴方法
【Amazonプライムビデオ】30日間無料体験あり
Amazonプライムビデオ『SPOTVチャンネル』では、MLB2026ポストシーズンを試合開催日に毎日1試合ライブ配信する。
プライム会員は追加料金なしで視聴でき、初めて登録する場合は30日間無料体験の利用が可能だ。
Amazonプライムビデオ登録方法
- Amazonプライムビデオのスポーツページへアクセス
- 視聴したい試合を選択
- 「ライブを観る 30日間の無料体験を始める」をタップ
- 支払い方法を入力
- 登録完了後、視聴を開始する
※無料体験終了後は月額600円(税込)で自動更新。
【SPOTV NOW】MLBポストシーズンもライブ配信
SPOTV NOW
『SPOTV NOW』では、2026シーズンもポストシーズンまでMLBを視聴できる。ポストシーズンの試合は全試合をライブ配信予定となっている。SPOTV NOW登録方法
- 「SPOTV NOW」の登録ページから希望するプランを選択
- 会員登録、またはSNSアカウント(Facebook・Apple・Yahoo!)を用いてログイン
- 各種情報を入力し、登録完了後すぐに視聴可能！
【MLB.tv】全試合配信！7日間無料体験あり
Amazon
まずはAmazonのMLB.tvチャンネルページにアクセス
- 「詳細を見る」をタップ。
- 支払い方法はクレジットカード、デビットカード、ドコモ・au・ソフトバンクの携帯決済、あと払いペイディに対応
- これで登録完了！すぐに視聴開始
なお、MLB.tvの登録は自分でキャンセルをしない限り、月額4,220円(税込)で自動更新となるので注意が必要だ。
Amazonページの「アカウントサービス」のPrime Videoチャンネルの管理からいつでもキャンセル可能だ。
※本ページは、Amazon.co.jpを宣伝しリンクすることによってサイトが紹介料を獲得できるアフィリエイトプログラムである、Amazonアソシエイト・プログラムの参加者です。

item.dc:creator: TJ French
item.description: Los Angeles Dodgers star Mookie Betts is entering the back half of his career, and while he isn’t at the MVP level that he once was from 2017-2022, Betts is still an extremely productive and successful player. item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers star Mookie Betts is entering the back half of his career, and while he isn’t at the MVP level that he once was from 2017-2022, Betts is still an extremely productive and successful player.
He has won three World Series titles with the Dodgers since joining the team in 2020, and he has four overall championship rings.
There has always been an ongoing debate on which team Mookie Betts favors between the Boston Red Sox and the Los Angeles Dodgers.
Betts came up with the Red Sox, and played six seasons in Boston, but 2026 marked Betts’ 7th season with the Dodgers, and he’s officially ready to call the Dodgers ‘his team’.
More MLB on Heavy: Freddie Freeman Makes Honest Admission About Los Angeles Dodgers World Series Aspirations
Mookie Betts Makes Heartfelt Admission to Put Red Sox-Dodgers Debate to Rest
Mookie Betts recently talked with The Athletic about which team he will state was ‘the one he played for’ when it’s all said and done:
“When I’m done playing, I’ll remember Boston, of course, But what I’ll really remember is if somebody said, ‘Oh, you played baseball, like who did you play with?’ These are the guys I’m going to say I played with,”
Betts also made a quick note about the fact that he believes he’s in the tail end of his career, which makes sense because he is 33 years old now with a growing family.
A couple of seasons ago, Mookie Betts added to his versatility as a baseball player by transitioning from right field to shortstop, which he has excelled at (all things considered).
There are still seven seasons left on Betts’ massive contract, which will expire when he’s 40, and he’s noted he plans to retire once that runs out.
More MLB on Heavy: Why Los Angeles Dodgers Fans Need to Watch Phillies-Braves Game on Thursday
Quickly Looking at Mookie Betts’ Career
Mookie Betts is an 8X MLB All-Star, AL MVP (2019), 4X World Series champion, 7X Silver Slugger winner, and 6X Gold Glover.
He’s almost certainly headed to the MLB Hall of Fame.
Betts has 314 career home runs, 982 RBI, 1237 runs scored, and a lifetime batting average of .288 over 1654 total games played.
In 2026, Mookie Betts batted .257 with 23 home runs, 25 doubles, and an OPS+ of 113.
Overall, it was a solid 2026 campaign for Betts after a very slow start at the plate.
More MLB on Heavy: Philadelphia Phillies Recent Pitcher Suddenly Makes Decision About Future

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Freddie Freeman Makes Honest Admission About Los Angeles Dodgers World Series Aspirations
item.dc:creator: TJ French
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers are still awaiting their National League Division Series opponent. They will find out on Thursday evening after the Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies conclude their Wild Card series. Regardless of the opponent, the Dodgers are poised and ready for their three-peat quest. That includes star infielder Freddie Freeman, who did not hold back about the team's World Series aspirations. More MLB on Heavy: Why Los Angeles Dodgers Fans Need to Watch Phillies-Braves Game on
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are still awaiting their National League Division Series opponent.
They will find out on Thursday evening after the Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies conclude their Wild Card series.
Regardless of the opponent, the Dodgers are poised and ready for their three-peat quest.
That includes star infielder Freddie Freeman, who did not hold back about the team's World Series aspirations.
More MLB on Heavy: Why Los Angeles Dodgers Fans Need to Watch Phillies-Braves Game on Thursday
Freddie Freeman's Latest Comments on Championship Window
Per The Athletic's Katie Woo, Freddie Freeman had this to say about LA's proverbial 'championship window':
"This window, we are going to try and keep open as long as we possibly can, but sports are sports; you never know when those windows will close."
Freeman also noted:
"I don't have that many years left of playing, so you take a step back and realize how special it is to come to the field every day for the chance to win a championship every year," Freeman said. "You look around, you've been with certain guys for those multiple titles, and you do realize that."
The Dodgers have won each of the last two World Series, and there hasn't been a team to three-peat as Champs since the turn of the century.
More MLB on Heavy: New York Mets Have 9 Free Agency Roster Decisions to Make This Offseason
Freddie Freeman Had Another Quality Offensive Season
Now that the regular season is in the books, we can take a look at how Freddie Freeman performed for the entire campaign, and to no surprise, he had another very solid offensive season.
Across 153 games played this season, Freeman batted .288 with an OPS+ of 118, 16 home runs, 32 doubles, and 167 hits.
He battled a few lingering injuries throughout the regular season, so the Dodgers hope that his health is not a factor in the upcoming NLDS against either the Braves or Phillies.
More MLB on Heavy: Toronto Blue Jays Star George Springer's Future in Jeopardy After Retirement Speculation

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA—While the Dodgers await the conclusion of the three-game Wild Card Series between the Philadelphia Phillies and Atlanta Braves, they’ll have plenty of time to look over their 26-man roster before Game One of the NLDS on Saturday.
Among those players on the bubble is top prospect rookie outfielder Josue De Paual, who, after a scorching two-week stretch while Shohei Ohtani was on the injured list, saw his chances of joining Los Angeles in October skyrocket.
Much of the discussion surrounding the Dodgers’ final NLDS roster spot has centered around Josue De Paula and Dalton Rushing potentially battling it out for the final left-handed bat off the bench.
While De Paula has shown plenty during his brief time in the majors and remains a major part of the Dodgers’ future, his potential inclusion on the NLDS roster would come with a clearly defined role. Rather than expecting the top prospect to become an everyday contributor in October suddenly, Los Angeles would primarily be looking to his bat in specific situations.
“I would say if he were to make it, it would just be as a bat,” manager Dave Roberts said.
That distinction is important because De Paula’s other tools are unlikely to get much use in a postseason series. He impressed during his September stint with the Dodgers after Shohei Ohtani was placed on the 15-day injured list, receiving most of his opportunities at designated hitter and showing the elite offensive potential that initially made him one of the organization’s most intriguing prospects.
Defensively, De Paula has acknowledged he wants to improve, but that could limit his opportunities in the field against a team the Dodgers expect to contend deep into October. His speed is another tool that could theoretically give Los Angeles an advantage, but Roberts doesn’t appear interested in using him as a pinch-runner.
“For me, that’s just really not his calling card,” Roberts explained. “So as far as on the bases, I just haven’t seen enough to supplant somebody else. But I’ve seen enough with the bat.”
That leaves De Paula’s bat as the primary reason for carrying him, and there is certainly an argument for it. The Dodgers have seen enough offensively to believe he can change a game with one swing, and limiting his responsibilities would let him focus on the one area where Roberts has already expressed confidence.
Still, that doesn’t necessarily mean De Paula would see significant playing time.
The Dodgers are also considering Dalton Rushing, who returned for their final regular-season series against the San Francisco Giants and went 0-for-3 with a strikeout. Rushing’s ability to provide more versatility could factor into how Los Angeles ultimately constructs the bench, making the final decision about more than which player has the better bat.
Roberts has also indicated that the Dodgers could consider adding Hyeseong Kim to the NLDS roster, though his inclusion would likely center on his speed and defense rather than his offense.
For De Paula, then, making the roster would be a significant accomplishment in itself. But don’t confuse a roster spot with a major October role. If the Dodgers carry him into the NLDS, the plan appears to be using him selectively as a dangerous left-handed bat rather than asking the 20-year-old to take on a regular role.
Still, a lot can happen, and things rarely go according to plan, and that could very well bode in De Paula’s favor. Whether it’s an injury or a double-switch situation, De Paula could play more than a small pinch-hit appearance, but for now, that appears to be his role moving forward this season.

item.content:encoded:
It's been two months since the Los Angeles Dodgers shocked the baseball world, trading for two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal.
The Dodgers were always viewed as the frontrunners to trade for the southpaw pitcher; however, it was still hard to believe when it actually happened.
With the Dodgers' postseason approaching, Skubal is poised to play a vital role in the team's quest for a three-peat. As for Skubal's former team, the Detroit Tigers, they're watching the postseason from home.
The Tigers received what they believed was the best package for Skubal. Detroit acquired outfielder Zyhir Hope and right-handed pitchers Brady Smith and River Ryan.
The Dodgers added an ace they hope they can lock up after the 2026 season, and the Tigers retooled their farm system with high-upside talent.
Los Angeles came out as the clear winners in the trade in present times, but Ryan is doing his best to ensure the Tigers come out as the winner when all is said and done.
On top of that, he took a subtle shot at the Dodgers while discussing his transition to the Tigers organization.
“I think the transition, as far as being traded on the injured list and then switching to a whole other organization and continuing through that process, I think Detroit made it really easy," Ryan said in a recent conversation with Just Baseball. "I think it was definitely a lot more hands-on with the Detroit organization. I feel like there was a lot more care involved, which was fantastic."
“They are being really involved in the day-to-day with me,” he added. “They’re all watching my outings, my bullpens. I mean, that’s really it. They’re just really trying to be as involved as they can on a day-to-day basis.”
Ryan also said the transition from Los Angeles to Detroit was pretty easy, since he's been traded before.
“I think since I’ve been through the trading process before, I kind of knew what to expect,” Ryan said. “Transitioning over to another team, meeting all new people, becoming acquainted with everybody. That was pretty easy because I’ve been through it before and I had a reference."
How Did River Ryan’s Dodgers Tenure Unfold?
Ryan was supposed to be a standout pitcher for the Dodgers. Unfortunately for him, his time in Los Angeles was riddled with injuries.
He missed the entire 2025 season recovering from Tommy John surgery and later dealt with minor setbacks like a hamstring issue, prompting the Dodgers to be extremely cautious with his workload.
Ryan, 28, will now do his best to pan out in the big leagues with the Tigers. He made two starts with the Tigers in late-September, alloiwng two runs over 4.1 innings with six strikeouts.

item.title: [Dodgers Nation] Mookie Betts Makes Feelings Clear on Dodgers vs. Red Sox Legacy
item.dc:creator: Nelson Espinal
item.description: Los Angeles Dodgers star Mookie Betts has a storied career with both the Dodgers and the Boston Red Sox, but he identifies more with one of those teams. Dodgers or the Red Sox? After multiple postseason runs and a legacy with the Dodgers, Betts made it clear he identifies more with the current Dodgers core than with any other team he has played for. “Going through the losses, going through all the ups and downs is why we are where we are today,” Betts said to The Athletic’s Katie Woo. “When I’m
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers star Mookie Betts has a storied career with both the Dodgers and the Boston Red Sox, but he identifies more with one of those teams.
Dodgers or the Red Sox?
After multiple postseason runs and a legacy with the Dodgers, Betts made it clear he identifies more with the current Dodgers core than with any other team he has played for.
“Going through the losses, going through all the ups and downs is why we are where we are today,” Betts said to The Athletic’s Katie Woo.
“When I’m done playing, I’ll remember Boston, of course. But what I’ll really remember is if somebody said, ‘Oh, you played baseball, like who did you play with?’ These are the guys I’m going to say I played with. That’s my team.”
For Betts, it must be hard to choose between the two franchises since he did well in both places and surely has fond memories of both, but he is known far more as a Dodger and a member of the current dynasty.
Mookie Betts’ History with the Dodgers and Red Sox
Betts has spent more time with the Dodgers, seven seasons, while playing only six years with the Red Sox, though arguably his best baseball came with the Red Sox, and that is where he ascended into superstardom.
In fact, in a statistical comparison, Betts earned 42.5 bWAR in Boston, while he got just 36.5 bWAR for the Dodgers.
He won an MVP with Boston, with a second-place finish, a sixth-place finish, and an eighth-place finish. He also got four Gold Glove awards and three Silver Slugger awards.
He has won three titles with the Dodgers, while he won only one with the Red Sox. Betts has four Silver Slugger awards and two Gold Glove awards.
Additionally, Betts moved from right field to shortstop as a Dodger, making a great transition that few players make in the latter half of their careers.
Given how things ended with the Red Sox, via a trade that was sudden and unexpected, the Dodgers have been a welcoming home for Betts.
He inked a 10-year contract and became the face of the franchise until Shohei Ohtani arrived, helping bring a title to an organization in a drought that struggled to get over the hump.
Betts is a certified Hall of Famer at this point with his resume, and it seems that when he makes it to Cooperstown, he will enter as a Dodger.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Mookie Betts Says Dodgers, Not Red Sox, Are His Team
item.dc:creator: Ricardo Sandoval; Unknown
item.description: Los Angeles Dodgers superstar Mookie Betts may have started his career in Boston, but he made it clear where he considers home. But what I’ll really remember is if somebody said, ‘Oh, you played baseball, like who did you play with?’ These are the guys I’m going to say I played wit
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers superstar Mookie Betts may have started his career in Boston, but he made it clear where he considers home.
After six seasons with the Red Sox and seven with the Dodgers, the 33-year-old believes he'll ultimately be remembered as a Dodger rather than a Red Sox player.
“When I’m done playing, I’ll remember Boston, of course. But what I’ll really remember is if somebody said, ‘Oh, you played baseball, like who did you play with?’ These are the guys I’m going to say I played with," Betts said to The Athletic regarding the Dodgers.
"That’s my team.”
Betts' first six seasons in Los Angeles couldn't have gone much better. He's helped the Dodgers reach the mountain top three times in that span, including in back-to-back seasons.
Betts' time in Los Angeles started with a bang, helping the Dodgers get the monkey off their back and win their first World Series title since 1988. After that, it was tough sledding for the team as a whole, but Betts played some of the best baseball of his career.
From 2020-23, Betts hit .282 with a .912 OPS, 113 home runs, 286 RBIs and 520 hits in 1,841 at-bats and 471 games.
That stretch was by far his best in Dodger blue.
Then, Betts transitioned to shortstop full-time in 2025, and has helped the team win consecutive World Series titles.
How Much Longer Will Mookie Betts Play for the Dodgers?
Betts' arrival ahead of the 2020 season helped usher in the new era of Dodger baseball.
Betts has done just about everything he wanted to do in Los Angeles, but even a run as successful as his with the Dodgers won't last forever. The 33-year-old opened up about the end of his career and reflected on what his time in Los Angeles has meant to him.
“I feel like I’m kind of on the tail end of what I signed up for,” Betts said. “I signed up in 2020 for that prime, and I feel like I got it. I got what I asked for, which is a team to go win.
“That’s why you know it’s so special with these guys. We’ve been together for four or five years, and I couldn’t imagine taking a field and not having those guys with me. Of course I want to play, but it’s almost like, well, if I don’t have my boys here, like, what am I doing?”
Bett's contract with the Dodgers runs through 2032. In the past, he has said he intends to retire at the end of this contract in 2032, when he is 40 years old.

item.title: [mlb.com] Could this top prospect be a postseason weapon for Dodgers?
item.dc:creator: Theo DeRosa

item.content:encoded:
On Sept. 13 at loanDepot park in Miami, the Dodgers rookie turned on a 98 mph fastball from Marlins righty Eury Pérez for a massive three-run home run: 108.2 mph off the bat and 416 feet into the right-field seats. In a game in which De Paula first walked and later roped a 101.9 mph double off the wall in right-center, it was the titanic homer that put Dodgers fans on notice.
Manager Dave Roberts seemed to think it was possible, saying the sweet-swinging lefty had earned the right to be “a part of the conversation” for the club’s NLDS roster when De Paula was optioned to Triple-A Oklahoma City on Sept. 23.
Here’s a look at how De Paula fared during his time in the Majors and what he could bring to the Dodgers during the 2026 postseason.
Power and plate discipline
In his 42 plate appearances with the Dodgers, De Paula put up some eye-popping offensive numbers: He posted a .323 batting average, a .500 on-base percentage and a .581 slugging percentage, scored seven runs and had seven RBIs. Most notable, though? De Paula drew 11 walks and struck out only five times.
Those 11 free passes rank as the third most in any Dodgers hitter’s first 11 career games, trailing only Andy LaRoche (2007) and Jim Gilliam (1953), who both had 12 walks.
Not only were opposing pitchers evidently cautious when pitching to De Paula -- who slashed .303/.401/.547 with 27 home runs this season for Double-A Tulsa -- but the lefty steadfastly refused to expand the zone. He swung at just 18 of the 97 out-of-zone pitches he saw for an excellent 18.6% chase rate, fitting right in on a Dodgers team whose 27.5% chase rate in 2026 ranked third best in the Majors. That’s not a fluke for De Paula, either: He drew 81 walks and struck out just 87 times this season in Double-A.
As good as his plate discipline is, De Paula can flat out mash, too. Twelve of the 26 balls he put in play in the big leagues were hard hit (95+ mph exit velocity), including five above 100 mph. Nine of those 26 (34.6%) registered as pulled-air contact; while De Paula’s Major League sample size is admittedly quite small, National League MVP favorite Pete Crow-Armstrong led MLB with a 34.0% pulled-air rate in 2026.
"He's just a special hitter," Roberts said. "Hitters don't see the ball that quickly out of hand; it's a gift. Just the ability to [limit] chase, I think that lines up in the postseason. And no moment is going to be too big for that kid."
Where does he fit in?
Evidently, De Paula’s offensive skill set could serve the Dodgers well in October. But what is his pathway to playing time?
That’s where things get a little difficult.
The rookie, who split his time with Tulsa between left and right field, made just two appearances in the field for the Dodgers, playing six total innings in left. Not willing to compromise what ranks as an average defensive outfield, the Dodgers plan to use De Paula as a designated hitter. There’s just one problem: Some guy wearing No. 17 currently occupies that spot.
Yes, Shohei Ohtani's presence will make De Paula’s path to postseason at-bats harder, although the Dodgers are certainly happy their superstar is back in the lineup. When De Paula was optioned to the Minors, it was as the corresponding move for Ohtani’s return from the injured list. Dalton Rushing's return from the IL two days later might also make it harder for De Paula to find postseason at-bats.
But there’s a reason De Paula became the first Dodger to bypass Triple-A and head right to the Majors since 2014. Used correctly -- presumably to face right-handed pitchers, against whom De Paula hit .314 with a 1.016 OPS in Double-A -- he can be a postseason weapon as a pinch-hitter or, if Ohtani is out of the lineup, at DH. The 6-foot-3, 185-pound De Paula has below-average sprint speed but still managed to steal 31 bases in 41 tries in the Minors this season, so he can be a threat on the basepaths as well.
While October baseball might prove to be overwhelming for the 21-year-old, De Paula could be a big piece of the Dodgers' success this postseason, whether it's in the NLDS or potentially further down the line.

item.title: [Dodger Blue] Freddie Freeman and Shohei Ohtani change routine ahead of NLDS
item.dc:creator: Matt Borelli
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers are getting a much-needed breather this week as they wait to see which team they will face in the National League Division Series, which begins Saturday with Game 1 at Dodger Stadium. The Dodgers will have their answer by the end of Thursday night as the Philadelphia Phillies and Atlanta Braves meet at Truist Park — the only Wild Card Series that reached a decisive Game 3. In the meantime, the Dodgers are using the time off to rest and prepare for their next opponent. The
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are getting a much-needed breather this week as they wait to see which team they will face in the National League Division Series, which begins Saturday with Game 1 at Dodger Stadium.
The Dodgers will have their answer by the end of Thursday night as the Philadelphia Phillies and Atlanta Braves meet at Truist Park — the only Wild Card Series that reached a decisive Game 3.
In the meantime, the Dodgers are using the time off to rest and prepare for their next opponent. The team has been going through workouts and simulated games at Dodger Stadium to stay sharp for when they resume play later this weekend.
As part of their on-field workouts, several Dodgers players got some swings in during batting practice. In a video shared by the team on X, the group of players who participated includes Shohei Ohtani, Freddie Freeman and Mookie Betts, among others.
Locked in for October. pic.twitter.com/RT5twoW3ED
— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 30, 2026
Ohtani taking swings during the bye week is an encouraging sign after he recently returned to the Dodgers following a stint on the 15-day injured list. He typically does not hit on the field, but has done it a few times throughout his tenure with the club, usually following a slump he’s trying to break out of.
For Freeman, the extra work could be pivotal in helping him get his swing back on track.
“Today is going to be a big day to see how BP goes,” Freeman said earlier this week. “Like I kind of told you guys a couple days ago, I feel like BP’s not going to go well today, just because of how my swing is right now. And then I’ll be able to start working on if I am blocking balls to left field in BP, then I can make those adjustments coming down.
“It’s hard to explain what’s going on in this head a lot of times, but it’s going to be big because I’m going to hit BP every single day on the field. I think that will help seeing balls velocity-wise, to be able to start moving it lower and lower and down toward the shortstop, and hopefully that will get my body in line with how I want it to work going into Saturday.”
The Dodgers had to manage Freeman down the stretch as he dealt with a right knee injury that affected both his offense and defense. He was kept out of the lineup for multiple games, but the Dodgers declined to place him on the injured list.
The time off did help Freeman improve, but the results didn’t follow. He closed out the season by batting just .226/.300/.278 over his final 30 games, and he hit just one home run in the final two months of the year.
The Dodgers are hopeful that the brief layoff will help Freeman reset mechanically and rediscover his rhythm at the plate just in time for the postseason.
Freddie Freeman incorporating 2024 World Series approach
Freeman has been exploring unorthodox ways to get back on track and recalled a key adjustment he made that led to his historic showing in the 2024 World Series.
“Just doing different work. I’m trying to find something that gets me results. We’re at the time where we’re just trying to get hot for five weeks here,” Freeman noted earlier this month.
“Kind of like I did in the World Series a couple years ago, I did the step-out move. That’s not sustainable over six months. (But) I’m not trying to find something that’s sustainable. I’m trying to find something that works for four weeks.”

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Dodgers Injury Updates Before NLDS: Shohei Ohtani, Freddie Freeman, Edgardo Henriquez

item.description: As the Los Angeles Dodgers prepare to embark on another October with sky-high expectations, there are a few stars who did not end the regular season at 100% health. item.content:encoded:
As the Los Angeles Dodgers prepare to embark on another October with sky-high expectations, there are a few stars who did not end the regular season at 100% health.
Superstars Shohei Ohtani and Freddie Freeman, and flame-throwing relief pitcher Edgardo Henriquez, have perhaps the biggest question marks surrounding them heading into the National League Division Series.
Here's the latest updates on all three players.
Shohei Ohtani Injury Update
Ohtani has dealt with nagging knee and biceps injuries for the majority of the season. His knee eventually shut him down from pitching ahead of the All-Star break, and his biceps injury resulted in the minimum stay on the 15-day IL, returning for a lackluster (5-for-21) final five regular season games.
General manager Brandon Gomes spoke on a Tuesday Zoom call with the media and had an update on the four-time MVP, and how his swing has been looking amid a much-needed break while the wild-card round finishes up.
“Everything is feeling great physically," Gomes said of Ohtani. "The swings, once he came back, overall were in a good place. And using these five days to continue to get reps and feeling good into this series is really important. But feels like he's in a great spot."
Manager Dave Roberts appeared to feel the same about Ohtani, and even went as far as saying that the man who hit just .245 during the second half of the season will still have a stellar postseason.
"I feel confident that you're going to see the best version of Shohei of the last two months," Roberts said. "I know that's sort of a low bar given his injury, but I do think that he's as healthy as he's been in quite some time. And every day from the training staff, it keeps getting better. So yeah, No. 1, he'll be a threat being in the lineup, but I do think that the performance piece will be what we're hoping for."
Freddie Freeman Injury Update
Freeman is no stranger to playing through injury, and has recently been dealing with right knee tendinitis that manifested itself in the form of a .184 batting average in the final 20 games he played of 2026.
"My body feels good,” Freeman said Tuesday. “I think that’s the main thing. I feel like it’s in a good spot to be able to do the work and hopefully fix my swing and everything that’s been going on the last couple months.”
Freeman was asked to compare his current pain level to past postseasons. Fans remember his heroics in the 2024 World Series —where he would later take home MVP honors — thriving through the Fall Classic despite a sprained ankle and broken rib cartilage.
“A couple of Octobers ago was probably 100 times worse, ailment-wise,” Freeman said. “I truly feel good right now, physically. So it’s on me now to figure out the mechanics of the swing in the next five days, and I have all the confidence in myself that I will figure that out by Saturday.”
Edgardo Henriquez Injury Update
Henriquez put up a 2.85 ERA across 60 innings of work this season, averaging a 100.8 mph fastball (in the 100th percentile among active pitchers), until lower back discomfort landed him on the injured list last month. He was activated off the IL this week.
“He’s trending really well at this point,” Gomes said. “His last live BP went well. He’s responding positively after he throws and isn’t feeling any lingering discomfort. We’ve still got a few steps to go. But if that all goes well, then yeah, the expectation is he’ll be on the roster.”
Roberts also made sure to acknowledge how pivotal the off-week was for his fireballer. Due to an excellent track record (a career 2.73 ERA in 86 regular season appearances), he could prove to be a crucial piece this October.
“I think he’s one of those guys that getting the bye has really benefited,” Roberts said. “He’ll throw another live or sim game to some hitters. ... Then he should be ready to go. And given the body of work, what he’s done, the unique skill set could be huge for us, will be huge for us.”

item.title: [yardbarker.com] Dodgers NLDS Notes: Edwin Díaz, Edgardo Henriquez & Starting Rotation
item.dc:creator: Matthew Moreno
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers earned the benefit of a postseason bye and now are reaping the full benefit as the Philadelphia Phillies staved off elimination to force the Atlanta Braves to a winner-take-all Game 3 in their Wild Card Series matchup. item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers earned the benefit of a postseason bye and now are reaping the full benefit as the Philadelphia Phillies staved off elimination to force the Atlanta Braves to a winner-take-all Game 3 in their Wild Card Series matchup.
The winner advances to face the Dodgers in the National League Division Series, which begins Saturday at Dodger Stadium. The start for time for Game 1 has not yet been decided as it hinges on whether or not the San Diego Padres or Chicago Cubs reach the NLDS to play the Milwaukee Brewers.
In the meantime, the Dodgers are spending the rest of the week going through workouts and simulated games, much like their approach in 2024 that proved beneficial.
The Dodgers avoiding the Wild Card Series this year has proven beneficial for multiple players dealing with an injury, including Edgardo Henriquez.
He missed the final two weeks because of lower back discomfort but has made steady progress in his recovery and is on track for the NLDS.
“We’ll get him some work this week. He’s trending really well at this point,” Dodgers general manager Brandon Gomes said on Tuesday. “His last live BP went well, he’s responding positively after he throws and isn’t feeling any lingering discomfort.
“We’ve still got a few steps to go, but if that all goes well, then yeah, the expectation is he’ll be on the roster.”
Elsewhere in the Dodgers bullpen, Edwin Díaz finished the regular season on a high note after returning from a stint on the 15-day injured list because of a neck issue.
“I don’t know if we could have asked much more out of Edwin. I think it was, like, a 50-plus percent strikeout rate when he came back,” Gomes noted. “Felt like each outing was more and more sharp, and looking more like himself.
“Feels like he’s in a great place right now, stuff out of hand is as good as it’s been all year, and we know that he has pitched in the hottest of hot games in the past, and in any role, especially in the postseason. He’s looked great and glad that he’s in the position that he’s in and was able to bounce back after the IL stint.”
Díaz threw five scoreless innings, allowed just one hit and one walk while collecting nine strikeouts across five appearances upon getting activated Sept. 18. While Gomes projected confidence, what may still be different for Díaz is he’s not relied upon as the primary closer.
Even without Shohei Ohtani pitching, the Dodgers are heading into the playoffs with a formidable starting rotation that consists of Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow. What order they will pitch in has not yet been decided.
Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said the team would not set their NLDS rotation until Thursday, at which point they would know whether the Braves or Phillies advanced.
“I say that because just trying to figure out opponent and the schedule going forward, not sure about game times and things like that. We’re having conversations but we’re not definitive yet,” Roberts explained.
“I think opponent certainly should matter, could matter. Talking to Mark Prior about where guys are at. To be honest, we could really put all four guys in a hat and run them out there. But I think there is going to be more thought behind it. We don’t need to make a decision right now, so really just trying to be clear and talk through it.”
Last year the Dodgers almost exclusively used Snell (Wild Card, NL Championship Series and World Series) as their Game 1 starter. Ohtani started against the Phillies in the opener of the NLDS.
One change from the 2025 postseason is Glasnow’s first appearance likely won’t come out of the bullpen during the NLDS due in part to a different schedule.

item.title: [heavy.com] Why David Stearns’ Pitching Philosophy Stands Between the Mets and Tarik Skubal
item.dc:creator: Terrance Biggs
item.description: New York Mets owner Steve Cohen is the richest in the MLB. He’s spent at least a billion dollars in contracts to bring a World Series trophy back to Queens. However, his money did nothing but return misery and hopelessness. Unlike his predecessors, the Wilpons, Cohen is more than eager to open his wallet and continue trying to bring talent to Flushing. Meanwhile, David Stearns, the president of baseball operations, faces criticism from both media and fans for free agent signings that have not be
item.content:encoded:
New York Mets owner Steve Cohen is the richest in the MLB. He’s spent at least a billion dollars in contracts to bring a World Series trophy back to Queens. However, his money did nothing but return misery and hopelessness. Unlike his predecessors, the Wilpons, Cohen is more than eager to open his wallet and continue trying to bring talent to Flushing.
Meanwhile, David Stearns, the president of baseball operations, faces criticism from both media and fans for free agent signings that have not been successful. With the exception of Juan Soto, who continues to excel, Stearns’ eye for talent seems to have suffered from astigmatism, where he cannot judge the proximity of the roster to becoming a winning one.
Yet, some believe that lefthander Tarik Skubal, in the estimation of many, could be the one to lead the Mets back to the playoffs. However, considering Stearns’ approach, the deal looks like a long shot. Stearns, in his season postmortem, discussed the need for starting pitching.
“I do think it is necessary for us to add to our rotation,” Stearns said. “We can do that in a variety of different ways. We’ve talked about this plenty before—you’d always love to add to the top of your rotation; any team would love to do that. Over the long term, what we need to do is develop pitchers at the top of our rotation, and I think we are proving we can do that, and we’ll continue to do that.”
On Baseball Night in New York, @chelsea_janes says “call me crazy” but she’d rather have two good starters opposed to getting just Tarik Skubal pic.twitter.com/STB6i2PTe2
— SNY Mets (@SNY_Mets) September 28, 2026
Making the Case
First, Skubal is a southpaw that the Mets need to break up their righty-dominant rotation. More importantly, his 2.72 ERA & 0.96 WHIP suggest that he continues to dominate pitchers, even after changing leads and settling into the Los Angeles Dodgers pressure cooker.
It makes sense to bring in an elite lefty to minimize the impact of Bryce Harper, Pete Crow-Armstrong, Kyle Schwarber, and Shohei Ohtani. Additionally, Skubal’s presence would also take the pressure off a bullpen that sorely needs a frontline starter to pitch into the seventh inning. Freddy Peralta was supposed to be the one, but he often struggled to escape the fifth.
Tarik Skubal has 10 Ks through 6 scoreless innings! pic.twitter.com/LOWMtaLuIf
— MLB (@MLB) September 26, 2026
Against the Grain
Stearns, during his time with Milwaukee, built his rosters on a mix of young talent, under-contract control, and not paying pitchers long-term. As a result, when news of Peralta sought a nine-year extension, his days in New York became shorter. Stearns, to his credit, continues to build a farm system that produces young talent.
Skubal presents a departure from all of that. First, he will command at least $300 million in a long-term contract. Next, Stesarns wants the rotation to still have room for the younger pitchers like Christian Scott, Nolan McLean, Zac Thornton, and eventually Jonah Tong. To sign Skubal, Stearns would need to completely change how he fundamentally views pitching, and that does not seem to be the case at all.
Danny Abriano of SNY outlined the perils of signing a veteran pitcher long-term.
“For every long-term, big-money deal to a pitcher 29 or older that works out (Max Scherzer’s seven-year deal with the Nationals looks incredible in retrospect, and the Yankees‘ deal for Max Fried is aging well), you can point to a whole bunch that didn’t or currently aren’t (Patrick Corbin, Jacob deGrom, Jordan Zimmermann, Felix Hernandez, and Corbin Burnes).”
Scherzer and Fried appear to be the few exceptions to the rule. Otherwise, it’s a dice roll on what type of arm you will get. On top of that, Skubal already underwent a medical procedure this season.
Mets fans see Skubal as their ticket to the playoffs. Similarly, some media do. However, the Mets, despite their abundant supply of cash, could look to other avenues.

item.title: [Dodgers Way] Dodgers babying Kyle Tucker in his first year had better pay off in October
item.dc:creator: Jordan Campbell
item.description: The calendar has flipped to October, and you know what means, it's time for another Kyle Tucker fluff piece. The saddest form of sports commentary that has become a trend in recent years is that when a star player has failed, some in the media believe it's the right time to coddle the individual and say anything other than the quiet part out loud. Kyle Tucker's first year with the Los Angeles Dodgers was a disaster, and no amount of spin is going to change that reality. Nonetheless, The Athletic
item.content:encoded:
The calendar has flipped to October, and you know what means, it's time for another Kyle Tucker fluff piece. The saddest form of sports commentary that has become a trend in recent years is that when a star player has failed, some in the media believe it's the right time to coddle the individual and say anything other than the quiet part out loud. Kyle Tucker's first year with the Los Angeles Dodgers was a disaster, and no amount of spin is going to change that reality.
Nonetheless, The Athletic's Katie Woo and Fabian Ardaya have some time on their hands this week, and what better time to talk about how Tucker can flip the script on his first year in LA. They want you to know that Tucker is aware of all the things that have been said about him this season, and like Mike Gundy talking down a claims from a reporter many moons ago, he wants you to know "that's not true."
Tucker is a man, he's 29, talk to him. That's what The Athletic did, and Tucker wants you to know that he's not a dementor from Harry Potter. Despite his struggles, and the noise that surrounded his contract with the Dodgers, he's had fun.
I’ve enjoyed my time here,” Tucker said. “Obviously, the better you play, the more fun you probably have, because that’s the whole reason why I’m here in the first place. But I’ve had a lot of fun here. The not-fun part about it is missing pitches and not being able to help the team throughout the year. Outside of that, I’ve had a blast.”
Dodgers' careful handling of Kyle Tucker will finally face the only test that really matters
The reality is these things can often resolve themselves. For everything that has gone wrong for Tucker with the Dodgers this season, if he's a hero during the playoffs, all will be forgotten.
Unfortunately, hope of Tucker simply flipping the switch because it's now playoff baseball may be misguided. Through 279 plate appearances in the playoffs, Tucker is slashing .233/.317/.376 with 58 strikeouts. In other words, during the playoffs, Tucker has been the exact disappointment that he's been with the Dodgers for the entire season.
If Tucker breaks that trend and is a difference-maker for the Dodgers during their playoff run, above all else, that will be the lasting image. Though, "Ifs" has been the biggest problem with talking about Tucker's run with the Dodgers.

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Dodgers Notes: Glasnow's Role, Freeman's Knee & More
item.dc:creator: Cody Snavely
item.description: LOS ANGELES, CA—The start of the 2026 National League Division Series is just two days away, and the Dodgers have spent the last couple of days getting their final work in before October officially begins. With Los Angeles enjoying the first-round bye, the extra time has allowed the team to rest, prepare, and get healthy while also giving us plenty to talk about from workouts. From Tyler Glasnow’s potential role and Freddie Freeman’s knee to the Dodgers patiently waiting to find out who they’ll
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA—The start of the 2026 National League Division Series is just two days away, and the Dodgers have spent the last couple of days getting their final work in before October officially begins.
With Los Angeles enjoying the first-round bye, the extra time has allowed the team to rest, prepare, and get healthy while also giving us plenty to talk about from workouts. From Tyler Glasnow’s potential role and Freddie Freeman’s knee to the Dodgers patiently waiting to find out who they’ll face in the NLDS, several interesting developments have emerged around camp.
So, with the weekend quickly approaching, here’s the latest from Dodgers camp as Los Angeles gets ready to begin its three-peat chase.
Tyler Glasnow Unlikely to Repeat His Bullpen Role From Last October for NLDS
While the Dodgers await the outcome of today’s final Wild Card game between the Phillies and Braves, they have begun laying the groundwork for their pitching staff ahead of Saturday’s NLDS opener.
While Dodgers manager Dave Roberts did not confirm the team’s starting rotation order for the series, he did allude to the fact that right-hander Tyler Glasnow likely won’t be used in relief, as he was during last NLDS against the Phillies.
A big reason is the scheduling of this year’s series compared to last season, with Games One and Two on back-to-back days rather than an odd day off between them.
“He’s one of four (starting pitchers),” Roberts began. “I think it’s a little different with the layout of the games in the DS, not playing in the Wild Card also. Could he factor in one of the first three games? Possibly.
“I would say most likely Game Four. I don’t see him out of the bullpen early. We’re going to talk through that in the next couple of days here.”
That makes a repeat of last year’s strategy unlikely. The Dodgers could still turn to Glasnow out of the bullpen later in the postseason if the situation calls for it, particularly in an elimination game, but for now, it appears his focus will remain on starting.
Still, Glasnow was elite in that role last season, tossing 1.2 scoreless innings between Games One and Two at Citizena Bank Park and proceeded to toss six more shutout innings in the Dodgers’ extra-inning walk-off victory in Game Four.
Freeman Says His Knee Is Feeling Good as He Looks to Reset Before the NLDS
Having the first-round bye for the Dodgers was seen as essential by many members of the organization and the media. Still, none preached for it more than Dodgers veteran first baseman Freddie Freeman, and that makes sense given his late-season struggles and apparent knee injury.
Freddie Freeman’s knee appears to be in a much better spot heading into the Dodgers’ NLDS matchup, giving him five full days during the postseason bye to focus on getting his swing back on track.
Freeman was held out of the lineup for multiple games late in the regular season, but the Dodgers never placed him on the injured list. While the extra rest helped his knee, his offensive struggles continued, as he hit just .226/.300/.278 over his final 30 games and .184 with a .513 OPS in September.
Still, Freeman isn’t using the knee as an excuse.
“My body feels good. I think that’s the main thing,” Freeman said Tuesday. “I feel like it’s in a good spot to be able to do the work and hopefully fix my swing.”
Freeman acknowledged the knee may have contributed to some bad habits at the plate, but ultimately blamed himself.
“I’ll never blame anything physical-wise for why I didn’t play well,” Freeman said. “I just didn’t play well the last couple of months of the season.”
Now, Freeman sees the five-day break as a valuable opportunity to reset without the pressure of immediately taking his work into a game.
“My knee’s in a good spot now, that’s why the bye week is huge,” Freeman said. “Personally, it’s huge for me that I’ve got five days to really work on the mechanics of my swing.”
With live at-bats against Dodgers pitchers planned during the break, Freeman will have plenty of time to iron out those mechanical issues before the NLDS begins Saturday.
Dodgers Keeping Three-Peat Talk in the Background, Focused on One Game at a Time
All that talk around Major League Baseball and throughout Los Angeles will be whether the back-to-back champion Dodgers can become the first National League team to three-peat.
And while that will be a major storyline following the Dodgers this October for every series they’re in, that is not the focus of the players and coaches in the clubhouse.
The three-peat has been on the Dodgers’ minds since last year’s World Series parade, but with the NLDS just days away, the players aren’t interested in adding that pressure to an already difficult task.
Max Muncy acknowledged the goal is there, but said the Dodgers are focused on preparing for their next series rather than thinking about the bigger picture.
“I mean, obviously it’s there, but it’s not something that we’re really focused on,” Muncy said. “We don’t need to be adding any extra pressure onto ourselves. When you talk about three-peating, you’re putting that extra pressure that doesn’t need to be there. Winning the World Series is already hard enough as it is.”
Freddie Freeman has a similar mindset, making it clear his attention is on the NLDS and nothing beyond it.
“Personally, I’m not thinking about three-peat,” Freeman said. “I’m thinking about the NLDS and whoever we play, and getting ready for that. I think if you think big picture in this moment, you’re going to lose sight of some things.”
Dave Roberts echoed his players, saying the Dodgers understand what’s at stake without needing to discuss it constantly.
“Our guys understand what’s at stake,” Roberts said. “I think for me, it’s balancing the importance, the opportunity that we have. Versus trying to add more pressure than there already is.”
The Dodgers know they have a chance to make history, but for now, the message throughout the clubhouse is simple: focus on the next series, not the three-peat.
Dodgers’ NLDS Opponent Still Up in the Air After Phillies-Braves Split
Later today, the Dodgers will finally know who they’ll face in the best-of-five NLDS that kicks off Saturday at Dodger Stadium, whether it’s the Phillies or Braves.
The Phillies rallied for a 4-3, 10-inning win over the Braves, tying the Wild Card Series and forcing a winner-take-all Game Three Thursday. That means the Dodgers’ eventual NLDS opponent will have to play three games in three days just to reach Los Angeles.
That’s a significant advantage for the Dodgers.
While Philadelphia and Atlanta are burning through their pitching staffs, Los Angeles is resting, preparing, and lining up its rotation. Whoever survives Thursday will arrive in Los Angeles having already played three high-pressure postseason games while the Dodgers have been sitting at home.
Philadelphia, in particular, had to dig deep Wednesday. Cristopher Sánchez threw 116 pitches over 6⅔ innings, while Andrew Painter recorded the final nine outs. If the Phillies advance, Zack Wheeler would presumably start Game Three, potentially affecting his availability for the NLDS opener.
That could be especially important considering Wheeler, Sánchez and Jesús Luzardo give Philadelphia one of the more formidable rotations in the postseason.
But Atlanta won’t escape unscathed either. Chris Sale already threw six innings in Game One, while Tyler Mahle delivered seven strong innings Wednesday. Both teams have used key starters and relievers, with one more game to go.
The Dodgers don’t have to win a Wild Card game. They don’t even have to play one. Their opponent does.
So while Los Angeles waits to find out whether it will be Philadelphia or Atlanta, it’s also watching its eventual opponent spend three games, three days, and a whole lot of pitching just to earn the right to come to Dodger Stadium.
The Dodgers’ NLDS opponent remains up in the air. The advantage of making that team play all three games, however, is already locked in.

Cody Snavely has been the co-editor of DodgersBeat and full-time host of the Bleed Los Podcast since February 2023. He has also written for multiple websites, such as Dodgers Way, Dodgers Low-Down, and Dodgers Tailgate. A Wilmington University graduate, Snavely is an avid Dodgers fan who uses his advanced baseball knowledge to keep fans updated on the latest storylines, rumors, and opinions on Dodgers baseball.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Dodgers notes: Offense, Freddie Freeman, Miguel Rojas
item.dc:creator: Andy Lane Chapman
item.description: As the Los Angeles Dodgers await the outcome of the final game between the Philadelphia Philles and Atlanta Braves to see who they will face in the NLDS, the team is busy working on keeping their bats and arms fresh and ready for the road to a three-peat that lies ahead. As Bill Plunkett of the OC Register notes, the last two championship wins were won mainly on the backs of the pitchers – the bullpen in 2024, and key starters in 2025. Could this finally be the year that the Dodgers win it by ha
item.content:encoded:
As the Los Angeles Dodgers await the outcome of the final game between the Philadelphia Philles and Atlanta Braves to see who they will face in the NLDS, the team is busy working on keeping their bats and arms fresh and ready for the road to a three-peat that lies ahead.
As Bill Plunkett of the OC Register notes, the last two championship wins were won mainly on the backs of the pitchers – the bullpen in 2024, and key starters in 2025. Could this finally be the year that the Dodgers win it by having their offense outslug the other teams?
"It would be nice to slug our way to a World Series one of these years," third baseman Max Muncy joked on the eve of another postseason run. "We can't keep letting the pitchers take all the credit, right?"
The offense has looked better in the month of September, and they hope to continue that and have those that weren't hitting join those that are. Plunkett has more thoughts from the players on how they're looking to perform in the playoffs here.
As Bill Shakin of the L.A. Times notes, the last two World Series runs have had signature moments from Freddie Freeman, and ponders if this playoff run will have the same.
"My body feels good," Freeman said. "I think that's the main thing. I feel like it's in a good spot to be able to do the work and hopefully fix my swing and everything that's been going on the last couple months."
Shakin goes on to cover Freeman's lackluster second half, and has more quotes from the man himself here.
As the team moves into its newest playoff era, one player is contemplating the end of his own. Miguel Rojas announced at the beginning of the season that he would be retiring at the end of this season. Now, he's not quite so sure. Maddie Chen of the L.A.Times talks about how Rojas is facing the possible end of his career.
"From this moment on, it will be kind of like a day-to-day thing," he said. "And you might get to know that I'm stepping away from the game in an Instagram post, or from me just saying goodbye on a video. I don't know. I don't know how it's going to be, but at this moment, I'm not 100% [certain]."

item.content:encoded:
El eficiente relevista cumanés Edgardo Henríquez continúa mejorando de los dolores en la espalda que lo llevaron a la lista de lesionados el pasado 14 de septiembre,
El gerente general de los Dodgers, Brandon Gomes, indicó que Henríquez ha avanzado hasta el punto de enfrentarse a bateadores en una sesión de práctica de bateo en vivo, informó el portal rotoworld.com.
Gomes señaló que la evolución del derecho de 24 años es positiva, lo que parece indicar que formará parte del róster del conjunto de Los Ángeles para la postemporada cuando comiencen su serie divisional de la Liga Nacional este fin de semana.
Leer también: Boston pierde un jugador esencial para lo que resta del comodín
Henríquez, especialista en situaciones de alta presión y dueño de potentes envíos, registró una sólida efectividad de 2.85 y una relación de 71 ponches por 25 bases por bolas en 60 entradas, antes de ingresar a la lista de incapacitados debido a molestias en la zona lumbar.
Cargado de un buen control y de una potente recta, que ha llegado a superar las 100 millas por hora, Henríquez se presenta como una pieza clave en el bullpen de los californianos, que buscan ganar su tercera Serie Mundial consecutiva. En criollo en la ronda regular tuvo marca de 4-1 y 2.55 de efectividad con 2 salvados.

item.title: [Dodgers Way] Dodgers get Edgardo Henriquez update as postseason bullpen picture comes together
item.dc:creator: Katrina Stebbins
item.description: One of many things that makes the Los Angeles Dodgers so infuriating to competitors is how lucky they get when it comes to injuries. Over their last three seasons, their pitching staff has been riddled with shoulder inflammation and elbow impingements, and so on — but they always seem to get their key players back exactly when they need them. They might have lost Blake Treinen in their last series of this season, but he's had a tough year and wasn't a lock for the postseason roster anyway. The r
item.content:encoded:
One of many things that makes the Los Angeles Dodgers so infuriating to competitors is how lucky they get when it comes to injuries. Over their last three seasons, their pitching staff has been riddled with shoulder inflammation and elbow impingements, and so on — but they always seem to get their key players back exactly when they need them.
They might have lost Blake Treinen in their last series of this season, but he's had a tough year and wasn't a lock for the postseason roster anyway. The real concern was for Edgardo Henriquez, who's been missing since September 14 with lower back discomfort.
Henriquez was officially activated from the IL on Tuesday, but his status ahead of the NLDS still seemed touch-and-go, given how fresh off injury he'll be with zero runway.
There are still boxes he has to check, but Dodgers GM Brandon Gomes said on Tuesday that he's trending the right direction. Katie Woo reported, "should he come out of all bye-week activities (live hitters, sim games, etc), he'll be on the NLDS roster."
The back end of the Dodgers' bullpen has no clear hierarchy right now, so Henriquez would be a welcome addition for later innings.
Edgardo Henriquez trending positively toward returning for Dodgers' NLDS
It's hard to guess what Dave Roberts' trust tree might look like heading into October. Tanner Scott, Edwin Díaz, and Tanner Scott are the obvious closing options, but Scott posted a 4.15 ERA in September, Díaz showed signs of life after his IL stint but still isn't truly trustworthy, and there's no telling if Sasaki will turn back into the lights-out closer he became last season.
The Dodgers used Henriquez as early as the third and as a late as extra innings over the course of the regular season, but he picked up two saves in nine games finished this year. His ability to throw 100+ MPH with regularity is his greatest asset, as long as he can control his pitches.
He was trending toward a more regular eighth- or ninth-inning role before he got hurt, as the Dodgers had to go with closers by committee with Díaz's absences and Scott struggling a little more. Henriquez has been effective anywhere between the seventh and ninth, with just a .191 batting average and .553 OPS against.
The Dodgers' bullpen being as shaky as it still is, the onus will be on the starters (again) to go as deep into games as possible, but Henriquez's presence should add a little more assurance.

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Freddie Freeman Using Bye Week to Retool His Swing for October
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA — Freddie Freeman knows exactly how he wants to spend the Dodgers’ five-day break before the National League Division Series.
It’s all about his swing, and getting it right for the playoffs.
Freeman spoke at length Tuesday about his late-season struggles, the work he plans to put in during the bye and why he feels confident he can get his swing where it needs to be by Saturday. He also talked about the Dodgers’ October experience, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and the example set by his father after the death of Freeman’s mother when he was a child.
Five Days to Work on the Swing
“My body feels good. I think that’s the main thing. I feel like it’s in a good spot to be able to do the work and hopefully fix my swing and everything that’s been going on the last couple months.
“I have a plan I’m going in with, and hopefully that will take care of itself throughout the course of the week where I’ll be in a good spot by Saturday.”
Freeman dealt with knee trouble during the second half, but he put the responsibility for his drop in production on himself.
“I’ll never blame anything physical-wise for why I didn’t play well. I just didn’t play well the last couple months of the season. That’s what I’m going to go with.
“Did I have some ailments with my knees? Yes, I did. I don’t know how much that attributed to it subconsciously, trying to do stuff where it didn’t hurt as much. There were times during the course of the last couple months where there would be a three- or four-day span where the knee was a problem and I couldn’t get into the front side, so maybe I created bad habits.
“But I won’t blame it on that. I just played bad.
“My knee’s in a good spot now. That’s why the bye week is huge for me personally. I’ve got five days to really work on the mechanics of my swing, and my knee’s in a good spot where I feel like I will be able to do that.”
Freeman planned to hit on the field every day, using batting practice to work through the changes before seeing live pitching later in the week.
“Today is going to be a big day to see how BP goes. I feel like BP’s probably not going to go well today just because of how my swing is right now, and then I’ll be able to start working on it.
“If I am blocking balls to left field in BP, then I can make those adjustments. There’s a lot going on in this head a lot of times, but it’s going to be big because I’m going to hit BP every single day on the field.
“I think that will help, seeing balls velocity-wise, to be able to start moving it lower and lower and down toward the shortstop. Hopefully that will get my body in line with how I want it to work going into Saturday.”
Back to Something That Worked in 2024
The physical picture is far better than it was during another recent October.
“A couple Octobers ago was probably 100 times worse ailment-wise. I truly feel good right now physically, so it’s on me now to figure out the mechanics of the swing in the next five days.
“I have all the confidence in myself that I will figure that out by Saturday.”
Freeman said he currently has no pain in the knee and expects rest after the season to be enough heading into next spring.
For now, he is going back to a swing thought that worked during the Dodgers’ 2024 championship run.
“It’s all evolved. Today I am going to kind of get more into my legs, and I’m going to try what I used in the World Series in ’24, kind of the step-out thought, so I’m not bending over and cutting off my swing.
“That’s the thought going into today. I’m very confident that’s going to help get things back in line throughout the course of the week.”
The bye also gives Freeman something he rarely gets during the season: time to work on a change without having to test it in a game a few hours later.
“I think the rest kind of takes care of itself mentally. I think that’s more of the mental rest.
“Physically, we’ll go out there and practice today, then we’ll play in some sim games the next two days and practice again. It’s baseball. You’ve got to play every day.
“But I think it’s more of the mental rest of not trying to figure out how to do something each and every day. That’s what’s going to be beneficial to me, where I can work on something today, go into tomorrow, work on something, then see how it translates into the live at-bats against real pitchers.
“It’ll be nice to work on something in BP and not have to take that into a game two hours later and see if it works. Today I can hone in on what I want to do in BP, and that’ll be it.
“Tomorrow I’ll come into BP and do that again, so I’ll have at least 400 swings going into tomorrow’s live BP of hopefully kicking out some of the bad habits.”
NLDS First, History Later
The Dodgers enter October with a chance to win their third straight World Series, but Freeman said his focus is much smaller right now.
“Personally, I’m thinking about the NLDS and whoever we play and getting ready for that.
“I think if you think big picture in this moment, you lose sight of some things. You’ve just got to take it one day at a time.
“We do understand the bigger picture, but if you’re looking at the bigger picture, you won’t be able to get to that big picture if you’re not focusing on the now.”
The Example Freeman Got From His Dad
One of Freeman’s more personal answers came when he was asked where his habit of taking responsibility and pushing through tough stretches came from.
Freeman pointed to his father, Fred, who raised three boys after Freeman’s mother, Rosemary, died when Freddie was 10.
“What I learned from my dad is someone who had his world turned upside down when my mom passed away when I was 10 years old, and he continued to take care of three boys and work and do the best he possibly could day in and day out and not be a ‘woe is me’ person.
“Obviously when I’m 10, I’m not thinking about that stuff. But as I’ve gotten older and I look back at what that man had to go through, the flip of a switch he had, he was a single dad of three and had his own business with his brother and still continued day in and day out to be the person he is and take care of us.
“As I’ve gotten older, I’ve realized there are no excuses. That man had every excuse in the book to do whatever he wanted in 2000, and he didn’t make an excuse. He went out there and did it each and every day.
“That’s my dad. Was he hard on me about my grades? Yeah, because I wasn’t that great in school. But he’s the best dad I probably could have had in that situation, with what he was going through and what we were all going through.
“What you think of him as a very down-to-earth man, that’s who my dad is. He’s a blessing.”
Plenty of Faith in Yamamoto and the Dodgers’ Staff
Freeman also had high praise for Yoshinobu Yamamoto as the right-hander heads into his third postseason with the Dodgers.
“He is special. From the first live BP that I saw when I faced him, it’s just special stuff, special command, the poise on the mound. Nothing’s too big for him.
“He’s one of those special pitchers that we get to watch day in and day out. It feels like he can put the ball wherever he wants, and we are very confident whenever he goes out there.
“Our pitching staff is pretty special, in my opinion. We’ve got four number ones rolling out there. It just goes on and on. Our pitching staff is most likely going to do it again like they did last year, and hopefully our offense can pick it up this year.”
Experience Counts in October
The Dodgers once again enter the postseason with one of baseball’s older position-player groups. Freeman sees the years this roster has spent playing deep into October as something that can help now.
“We’ve started in February overseas the last couple years and ended up winning the World Series. We know what’s going to be happening in the playoffs. We know what’s going to be thrown at us, the atmospheres.
“I think experience is huge in this. We’ve played a lot of baseball. We’ve been together a long time. We know what it takes.
“I think experience is definitely on our side going into this.”
For Freeman, though, the first order of business remains the same one he laid out at the start of the interview.
Five days. A healthy knee. Plenty of swings.
And a chance to get everything lined up before Saturday.
More Dodgers Coverage:
Have you subscribed to the Bleed Los Podcast YouTube channel? Be sure to ring the notification bell to watch player interviews, participate in shows & promotions, and stay up to date on all Dodgers news and rumors!
A lifelong baseball fan, Webb has been going to Dodger games since he moved to Los Angeles in 1987. His favorite memory was attending the insane Game 3 of the World Series in 2025 and hugging random Dodgers fans after Freddie’s walkoff homer. He has been writing for Dodgersbeat since 2020.

item.title: [roundtable.io] Freeman Uses Dodgers Break to Repair His Troubled Swing
item.dc:creator: Eduardo Solano

item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers first baseman Freddie Freeman is grinding through a structured hitting routine to shed poor habits and reclaim his elite offensive mechanics.
The Dodgers are resting since the end of the regular season on Sunday and Saturday’s National League Division Series opener against the Philadelphia Phillies or Atlanta Braves, providing Freeman with valuable recovery and preparation time.
Ready for the road ahead
According to Dodger Blue, Freeman said before Tuesday’s workout that his body felt good. He downplayed any lingering knee concerns and shifted his attention toward correcting a swing that has troubled him for the past couple of months.
Freeman had not started hitting Tuesday because the Dodgers held meetings first. He planned to begin afterward, take hitting practice every day and follow a structured routine designed to prepare him for Saturday.
“My body feels good. I think that’s the main thing,” Freeman noted.
“I feel like it’s in a good spot to be able to do the work and hopefully fix my swing and everything that’s been going on the last couple of months.
“So I have yet to hit today because we just had some meetings, and we’ll get going here after I get done with this. I’ll be hitting BP every day I got a plan going in, and hopefully that will take care of itself throughout the course of the week, where I’ll be in a good spot by Saturday,” Freeman continued.
The first baseman hit .288 with 16 home runs, 70 RBIs and a .792 OPS in 153 games this season. He struggled in September, hitting .184 with one home run and seven RBIs in 20 games.
No excuses for Freeman, Dodgers
Freeman refused to use his physical condition as an excuse. He acknowledged that knee problems occasionally prevented him from properly moving onto his front side during three-or-four-day stretches.
Those limitations may have subconsciously caused compensations and created poor habits, but Freeman accepted responsibility for his performance.
He believes the break is especially important because his knee feels strong enough to handle the work required to repair his mechanics.
“I’ll never blame anything physical-wise for why I didn’t play well,” Freeman said.
“I just didn’t play well the last couple months of the season. That’s what I’m going to go with. Did I have some ailments with my knees? Yes, I did. I don’t know how much that contributed to subconsciously trying to do stuff where it didn’t hurt as much.”
Freeman also views the layoff as more beneficial mentally than physically. The Dodgers practiced Tuesday, scheduled simulated games for the following two days and planned another practice afterward.
Instead of testing an adjustment during hitting practice and immediately carrying it into a game two hours later, Freeman can repeat the change over several days before facing teammates in live situations.
He planned to concentrate on specific details Tuesday, repeat that work Wednesday and take at least 400 swings before Wednesday’s live hitting practice. The goal is to eliminate habits developed during his difficult stretch.
“I think the rest kind of takes care of itself,” Freeman noted.
“I think that’s more of the mental rest. Physically, we’ll go out there and practice today, and then we’ll play in some sim games the next two days and practice again.
“Baseball, you’ve got to play every day. I think it’s more of the mental rest than not trying to figure out how to do something each and every day,” Freeman added.
Freeman recalled dealing with physical issues approximately 100 times worse during that postseason.
“A couple of Octobers ago was probably 100 times worse,” Freeman emphasized.
“Ailment-wise, I truly feel good right now. Physically, it’s on me now to figure out the mechanics of the swing in the next five days. And I have all the confidence in myself that I will figure that out by Saturday.”
Freeman’s accountability
Freeman acknowledges the injury’s possible influence without allowing it to become an excuse.
His preparation reflects discipline and confidence. Freeman does not expect his swing to improve without concentrated work, repetition and honest evaluation.
He also understands how to use experience constructively. Rather than simply attempting to recreate past success, Freeman is identifying which previous adjustments could solve his current mechanical problems and help the Dodgers win another World Series.
That combination of resilience, responsibility and attention to detail has helped him respond to difficult stretches throughout his career. Freeman believes his body will cooperate and trusts himself to correct his swing before Saturday.

item.title: [Dodgers Way] Projecting the Dodgers' NLDS roster with Josue De Paula, bench shuffle
item.dc:creator: Katrina Stebbins
